transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, nice to meet you too, Doc. I'm here because... well, my family, everyone really, they keep saying I’ve been doing too much. But to me? It just feels like I’m the only one left with enough drive to actually get anything done around here. We've got this big move to handle, and I'm taking care of all that, plus I'm rebuilding the new garage. I have to do it right, you know? 

Actually, speaking of the garage, you wouldn't believe the lumber they try to sell you these days. I was down at the hardware store Tuesday, and the two-by-fours were so warped they looked like rocking chair runners. I told the kid working the aisle—must have been nineteen, tops—I said, "If you tried to build a wall with this, it'd look like a funhouse." He just stared at me. Kids today, they just don't know how to work with their hands anymore. My grandson is the same way, always staring at that tablet of his... playing those games where you just tap the screen. I don't see the point. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Right, the move, the garage... and I'm organizing things at church, too. The committee is practically useless without me pushing them along. And on top of it all, I'm still at the plant. I do industrial mixing and blending, have for years, and I still have to be there to show the younger fellows at work how the job actually ought to be done. If I don't watch them, they'll mess up the calibration. We had a guy back in '94, didn't check the grinding pressure, ruined a whole silo of material. Took us three weeks to clean the dust out of the vents. It got into my truck, too, a blue Ford I had back then. Great truck. 

So... yeah, I'm just getting things done, but they made me come in to talk to you about it.
Have you been having problems with your memory lately?

Memory? No, no, my memory's sharp as a tack. I mean, I can remember things from way back, clear as day. Like that blue Ford I mentioned... 1988 F-150, straight six engine. You couldn't kill that truck. I used to take it up to the lake on weekends. We had this little cabin up there, well, more of a shack really, but we loved it. The water was so clear you could see the rocks on the bottom. We'd fish for bass right off the dock. My buddy Tom, he caught a five-pounder out there once. Tom... he moved out to Arizona a few years back. Says the dry heat is good for his joints. I don't know about that, I think I'd miss the changing seasons. The leaves turning in the fall... there's nothing like it. But yeah, no, my memory is just fine. Why, did someone say I was forgetting things?
Have you been needing much less sleep than usual lately?

Sleep? Well, I haven't really noticed needing any less, no. I mean, I sleep when I need to, you know? Usually, I'm up before the sun anyway, always have been. My dad was the same way. He used to say, "The best part of the day is before the rest of the world wakes up to ruin it." He was a milkman, actually. Back when they still delivered milk in those glass bottles right to your porch. You remember those? They had that little paper cap on top. In the winter, the cream would freeze and push the cap right up out of the bottle. We used to fight over who got to eat the frozen cream... tasted like ice cream if you put a little sugar on it. Dad had this route that took him all the way out past the county line. Sometimes he'd let me ride along in the truck. It smelled like cold metal and sour milk, but I loved it. We'd listen to the radio... mostly baseball games. I still listen to the games on the radio sometimes. It's better than TV, you have to use your imagination. But yeah, no, sleep hasn't really been an issue.
Have you been feeling unusually cheerful or high lately?

Cheerful? High? I don't know about cheerful, but I've been feeling... well, I feel ten feet tall. Like I've got all the answers and everyone else is just dragging their feet. I mean, I'll be joking around, feeling great, but then somebody will ask me some stupid little question and I just snap. Like my wife, or my boy, they'll interrupt me when I'm drawing up the plans for the garage and I just tell them, you either need to get on board with what I'm doing or get out of my way! 

Speaking of getting out of the way, you should see the traffic out on Route 9 these days. Used to be you could cruise all the way into town without hitting a single red light. Now? They put in three new subdivisions out past the old drive-in theater, and it's just bumper to bumper. The drive-in... man, we used to go there every Friday night when I was in high school. You could fit six people in the trunk of a Buick if you knew how to pack 'em right. We'd watch those old monster movies, the ones where the zipper on the rubber suit was still showing. We thought it was the funniest thing in the world. We'd get popcorn that tasted like cardboard and those big sodas in the wax paper cups. They don't make cups like that anymore. Now everything is plastic. Plastic this, plastic that. It's ruining the oceans, you know. I saw a documentary about it on public television. The turtles... they think the plastic bags are jellyfish. It's a shame, really, what we're doing to the planet. But anyway, yeah, I've just been feeling like I'm the only one who knows what's going on, and everyone else is just in the way.
Have you had any recent medical illness or brain problem, like a stroke or head injury?

Medical illness? Stroke? No, nothing like that. My brain's working better than ever, actually. I haven't been to a hospital since... well, since they took my appendix out back in '92. Or was it '93? It was right around the time the Blue Jays won the World Series, I remember that much because I was watching the game on this tiny little TV they had mounted up in the corner of the hospital room. Joe Carter hit that walk-off home run... man, what a moment. I used to play a little baseball myself, you know. Third base. They called me the "Hot Corner" because nothing got past me. I had this old leather mitt that I oiled every single week. Smelled like neat's-foot oil and dirt. You can't buy a glove like that anymore, everything now is synthetic. Just like those plastic cups I was telling you about. It's all connected, really. The synthetic gloves, the plastic in the ocean, the way people just don't take pride in their work anymore. Back when I was at the plant, running the grinders, you had to know your machine. You had to feel the vibration in the floor to know if the mix was right. But no, no head injuries or strokes or anything. Why, do I look like I had a stroke?
Have you been getting lost in places that should be familiar to you?

Lost? Me? No, no, I know exactly where I am and where I'm going. Always have. I've got an internal compass, like a homing pigeon. You know, they used to use pigeons to carry messages during the war. Remarkable creatures, really. People call them "rats with wings" now, but they saved lives. My uncle was in the Signal Corps, actually. He used to tell stories about the equipment they lugged around... radios the size of a suitcase. Now everyone's got a computer in their pocket. It's too much, if you ask me. People walking around, staring at their hands, bumping into each other. Nobody looks up at the sky anymore. The sky out past the county line, where my dad used to drive the milk truck, it was something else. You could see every star. So no, I don't get lost. I know every backroad in this county better than the people who paved them.
Have people been telling you that you’re talking more than usual?

Well, yeah, I suppose. Once I start explaining what needs doing, the words just keep coming, you know? My family, they complain that I talk over them so fast they can’t even tell me to stop. But I've got a lot of important things to get out! It's like I'm an auctioneer. You ever listen to those guys? Man, they can really rattle it off. We used to go to the livestock and equipment auctions out past the county line when I was a kid. My dad would bid on these old tractors, International Harvesters, mostly. Red as a candy apple. The sound of those old engines, that deep, heavy chug-chug-chug... you just don't hear machinery like that anymore. Now it's all electric this and hybrid that. Silent. You can't even hear a car coming up behind you in the grocery store parking lot! I almost got clipped by one of those little silent cars at the supermarket last Tuesday. And don't get me started on the supermarket, they moved the coffee aisle clear to the other side of the building and didn't put up a single sign to tell anybody where the Folgers went.
Have you ever had another period in your life when you felt this same way?

Another period? Well, I don't know, maybe? I mean, I always feel pretty good, but this... this is like my engine's been overhauled and running on premium fuel, you know? Premium fuel. I used to go to this old filling station on Route 9, back when they actually pumped your gas for you. Guy named Earl ran it. He had this little bell that would ding-ding when you rolled over the black hose, and he'd come out with a rag in his back pocket, wipe down your windshield, check your oil. Full service, they called it. Now you gotta freeze your hands off pumping it yourself, and half the time the screen on the pump is broken or asking if you want a car wash. Car washes! They used to have high school kids doing car washes on Saturdays to raise money for the band uniforms. My nephew played the trombone in the marching band. Big, brass thing. He was always complaining about how heavy it was to carry in the summer heat, especially during the Fourth of July parade. They always marched right down Main Street, right past the old courthouse with the clock tower. They don't make clocks like that anymore, all gears and heavy weights. It's all digital now, just blinking numbers. Blinking numbers everywhere you look. But, uh, what were you asking me? About feeling this way? I don't know, I just feel like I've got a lot of energy right now.
How long have you been feeling this unusually energized and driven?

Well, I'd say it's been about a month now. Ever since they made us start packing up to leave the old house. It's a shame, really, having to leave that place. The foundation was solid block, not like the cheap poured concrete they use in these new subdivisions. You know, I used to work the big industrial mixers, grinding and blending the aggregates for concrete down at the plant. Heavy work, dusty work. You'd come home and blow your nose and it would be gray. But we made good material. Built half the county with it. The bridges, the retaining walls over by the river... The river used to flood every spring before they put in the dam. I remember one year the water came right up to the porch of the old Miller place. They had these beautiful weeping willows in the front yard, just drinking up all that water. Willows are funny trees, they'll find a water pipe and crack it right open if you're not careful. Roots just snake their way in looking for a drink. Kind of like how I feel right now, just reaching out, ready to go, you know? But yeah, about a month, since we had to start moving out.
Have your family noticed that your memory or thinking has changed recently?

My memory? Well, I haven't noticed anything wrong with it. I mean, my daughter, she's always harping on me about forgetting where I put my keys, but who doesn't do that? Keys are small, they slip right down into the couch cushions. We had this old plaid couch when she was growing up, ugly thing, green and orange. But comfortable! Man, you could fall asleep on that thing in five minutes flat. We bought it at a yard sale down the street from this couple who were moving to Florida. Florida! Too hot for me. All that humidity, makes you sweat just standing still. And the alligators, you hear about those alligators crawling right up into people's swimming pools? Imagine waking up and finding a ten-foot reptile taking a dip in your backyard. They got those thick scales, like armor. Reminds me of the heavy equipment we used to use down at the mixing plant, big armored machines. You had to grease the joints on those things every single day or they'd seize up on you right in the middle of a job. Nothing worse than a seized bearing when you've got a deadline. But no, my memory is sharp as a tack. I can remember the serial number off my first car, a '68 Chevy. So I don't know what they're complaining about.
Before this past month, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt this unusually energized and driven for several days in a row?

Another time? Well, I don't know, maybe? I mean, I've always been a hard worker. You don't last long at the plant if you don't have the drive. The drive... that's what my old foreman used to say. "You gotta have the drive, boys!" He was a tough old bird, missing half his left index finger from a bandsaw accident back in the seventies. The seventies... man, those were different times. You could get a burger, fries, and a shake for under two bucks. We used to go to this drive-in place on Friday nights, they'd bring the food right out to your window on a little tray that hooked onto the door. You had to be careful rolling the window up, though, or the whole thing would spill. My buddy Frank spilled a whole strawberry shake on the interior of his Mustang once. Red interior, too, so you couldn't really see the stain, but the smell... it smelled like sour milk in there for a month. He tried everything to get it out, baking soda, vinegar, you name it. Vinegar is great for cleaning, you know. My mother used to wash the windows with vinegar and newspaper. Said it didn't leave streaks like those chemical sprays. Newspapers used to be so thick, especially the Sunday edition. You'd spend half the morning just reading the comics. Peanuts, Garfield, Family Circus... I always liked the ones with the little dotted lines showing where the kid ran all over the neighborhood. Just like me right now, going a mile a minute! But, uh, what did you ask me? About feeling energized before? I don't know, I've always had a lot of energy.
Have you started any new medicines or drugs recently?

New medicines? No, no, I haven't started anything new. I take my blood pressure pills, always have. The little white ones. They changed the shape of them a few years back, used to be round, now they're sort of oval. Oval... you know, like a football. I used to love watching football on Sundays. The old gridiron. We had this high school coach, Coach Henderson, he made us run drills until we puked. Tough as nails, that guy. He drove this old beat-up Ford pickup, rust all along the wheel wells. You see a lot of rust around here because they salt the roads so heavy in the winter. Salt eats right through the metal if you don't wash it off. We used to use a special sealant on the metal chutes at the mixing plant to keep the aggregate from wearing them down too fast. You had to reapply it every six months or the friction would just grind the steel down to nothing. Steel is strong, but friction... friction always wins eventually. Just wears things away. Kind of like my joints these days, knees popping every time I stand up. But no, no new drugs or anything like that. Just the usual stuff.
Before this past month, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt unusually energized like this for several days in a row?

Didn't you just ask me that? I swear we just talked about this. Like I was trying to say, I really couldn't tell you if I had times like this before. I don't know, I've just always been a go-getter. You know who else was a go-getter? My brother-in-law, Dave. He sold vacuum cleaners door to door back in the eighties. Those big heavy Kirbys. You ever use a Kirby? Built like a tank, those things. Heavy metal casing, a real solid motor in 'em. Not like the cheap plastic junk they sell today. Everything is plastic now. Plastic bags, plastic bumpers on cars... I remember when cars had real solid chrome bumpers. You get in a fender bender with a '57 Chevy, you'd barely leave a scratch on the bumper, but you'd absolutely total whatever plastic thing they're making nowadays. My neighbor drives one of those little plastic cars. A blue one. Parks it right on the property line, drives me up the wall. I keep telling him, 'Move it over a foot, Bob!' But he's deaf in one ear from his time in the artillery. Artillery is loud, man. Shakes your teeth right out of your head. Makes the ground vibrate... just like the big crushers at the plant. But anyway, yeah, I don't really remember any specific times like you're talking about.
Has there ever been another time in your life when other people told you that you were acting like this?

Other people telling me? No, nobody's ever said anything like that to me. People used to just mind their own business, you know? Good fences make good neighbors, that's what Robert Frost said. We read him in a literature class I took back at the community college. I only went for a couple semesters, thought about getting a business degree, but then the job at the mixing plant opened up. Good money, union benefits. The union was really strong back then. Local 402. We'd have these meetings down at the VFW hall on Elm Street on Tuesday nights. They served this terrible burnt coffee out of a big silver percolator. Those old percolators always made the coffee taste like aluminum. Aluminum is a funny metal. We used to blend these aluminum oxide powders for polishing compounds at the plant. Real fine dust, gets absolutely everywhere. You'd blow your nose at the end of the shift and the tissue would be sparkling. Sparkles... like the paint on those expensive bass boats. Guys take those out on the lake on weekends, spend twenty thousand dollars just to catch a two-pound fish. Fishing is way too slow for me anyway, sitting out there baking in the sun just waiting for a bobber to move. I like to keep moving, keep my hands busy. But yeah, to answer your question, nobody's ever told me I was acting any kind of way.
Before this month, was there ever another time in your life when you had several days of this same kind of unusually high energy?

I... wait, are you asking me that again? I feel like I'm stuck on a merry-go-round here. We just went over this, didn't we? I mean, I really don't think so. I don't remember any other time. Like I said, I've always been a guy who likes to keep moving. Moving... you know, kinetic energy. That's what they call it in physics. We had to learn a little bit about that at the plant, how the kinetic energy of the grinding wheels transferred to the aggregate. If the wheels spun too fast, they'd overheat and you'd smell this awful burning rubber smell. Rubber is amazing stuff though, comes right from trees down in South America. They tap them like maple trees up in Vermont. I went to Vermont once, for a fall foliage tour with my late wife, Brenda. Beautiful colors, all reds and oranges. Orange is a tough color to pull off, unless you're wearing hunting gear. I used to go deer hunting with my uncle when I was a teenager. He had this old lever-action Winchester rifle, kicked like a mule. Left a bruise on my shoulder the size of a grapefruit. Grapefruits are too sour for me, honestly. I prefer a nice sweet navel orange. But no, I don't recall any other time with this kind of energy. I'm just... I'm just feeling good right now, you know?
Has this past month caused serious problems at home or at work?

Well, it hasn't been great, I'll tell you that. At work, they actually pulled me off the floor after a safety incident. Just a little misunderstanding with the mixing equipment, but safety first, right? That's what they always say. We used to have these big yellow signs all over the plant: 'Safety First.' Yellow is a good color for that, really catches the eye. Like school buses. Did you know school buses are that specific shade of yellow because it's the easiest color to see in the early morning light? My cousin drove a school bus for thirty years. Thirty years! Can you imagine dealing with screaming kids for that long? Kids these days are always on their phones anyway, not even looking out the window. When I was a kid, we'd play games, you know, punch buggy or whatever. Volkswagen Beetles, they don't make them like they used to. Classic cars had character. Anyway, at home, things are a mess too. My wife and the kids, they basically stopped trusting me with anything. They won't let me make decisions about the money, they don't want me driving, they even took over planning this move we're supposed to be doing. They said things just got out of hand. Hand... you know, human hands are incredibly complex. All those tiny bones and tendons. I read an article once about how surgeons have to practice on grapes to get their hands steady enough. Grapes are mostly water, you know. Good for hydration. But yeah, it's caused some real headaches, both at the plant and at the house.
Have you been using any alcohol or recreational drugs lately?

No, I don't touch any of that. Never had a taste for drugs, and I haven't had a drink in... well, a long time. Used to grab a beer with the guys after a shift at the plant, sure. We'd go down to this place called O'Malley's. They had this beautiful old Wurlitzer jukebox in the corner, played actual vinyl 45s. You just don't see records much anymore, do you? Everything is digital now, floating around in the cloud or whatever they call it. I still don't really understand how a cloud holds information. Real clouds are just water vapor, condensation. You look up on a summer day and see those big puffy cumulus ones, they look like cotton candy. I used to buy cotton candy for the kids at the county fair when they were little. It's just spun sugar, really. Melts the second it hits your tongue. Terrible for your teeth, though. My dentist, Dr. Aris, he's always lecturing me about sugar. He's got these huge hands, feels like he's shoving a baseball mitt in my mouth when he checks my molars. But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right. No, no alcohol or drugs for me.
Have you had any recent changes in your blood pressure medicine?

Blood pressure medicine? No, I haven't had any changes to that. Same little white pill I've been taking for years. They make those pills so tiny though, they're hard to pinch out of the bottle with my thick fingers. Pinching... you know, crabs have incredible pinching power in their claws. I went crabbing once down in Maryland with my brother-in-law. You just tie a raw chicken neck to a piece of string and drop it in the water. Chicken is getting so expensive these days at the grocery store, though. Used to be the cheapest meat you could buy. Now everything is expensive because of inflation. A dollar just doesn't stretch like it used to. They used to make dollar bills out of silver certificates, backed by actual silver in the vault. Silver tarnishes, though, you have to polish it to keep it shining. I did a lot of polishing at the plant, actually, getting the metal components smoothed out on the line. You use a high-speed buffing wheel and a special compound for that. The compound smells a bit like wet clay. Clay is what they make bricks out of, baking them in massive kilns... but anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, the blood pressure medicine is exactly the same. No changes.
Have you ever had a period in your life when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Depressed? Two weeks? No, I don't think so. I've never really been one to get down in the dumps like that. I mean, everyone has a bad day here and there, sure, but not for weeks on end. Weeks... you know, a fortnight. They still use that word over in England, a fortnight. Fourteen nights. I've always wanted to go to England, see the Tower of London and all that history. History is fascinating, isn't it? The way things were built hundreds of years ago without any of the modern machinery we have today. Like the pyramids in Egypt! How did they move those massive stone blocks? Some people say it was aliens, but I think they just had a really clever system of ramps and pulleys. Pulleys are a simple machine, really. We used a lot of pulleys and hoists at the plant to lift the heavy mixing vats. If one of those cables snapped, watch out. That's why they had all those safety inspections. The inspector, this guy named Gary, he was a real stickler. He'd walk around with his little clipboard and his hard hat, checking every single bolt. Hard hats are important. They save lives. I always wore mine, even when it was hot and sweaty in the summer. Summer heat can really take it out of you, make you feel sluggish. But no, not depressed. I've never had a stretch like that where I just felt low all the time.
Before this past month, did you ever have another time in your life when you felt this same way for at least a week?

Felt this way before? For a whole week? No, I don't think so. This is really the first time. A week goes by so fast lately anyway. Seven days used to feel like a lifetime when you were working the line, though. We worked six days a week at the plant sometimes, during the busy season. The overtime pay was good, time and a half. I saved up all my overtime and bought a '68 Chevy Impala. Beautiful car. It had this deep blue paint job, almost like the ocean. I've never actually been out on the real ocean, though. I always wanted to take one of those big cruises. You see them on TV, those massive ships with swimming pools and all-you-can-eat buffets right on the deck. I always wonder how a boat that heavy even floats. Displacement, I guess. Archimedes' principle. We learned about that in a physics class I took at the community college back in the seventies. The professor had this wild white hair, looked exactly like Albert Einstein. Einstein was a genius, you know. He figured out relativity with just a chalkboard and some chalk... but wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right. No, I've never had a week where I felt like this before.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
doctor.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because everyone says I’ve been doing too much, but to me it feels like I’m the only one with enough drive to get the move handled, rebuild the new garage right, organize things at church, and still show the younger fellows at work how the job ought to be done.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code.

patient.answer:
Well, nice to meet you too, Doc. I'm here because... well, my family, everyone really, they keep saying I’ve been doing too much. But to me? It just feels like I’m the only one left with enough drive to actually get anything done around here. We've got this big move to handle, and I'm taking care of all that, plus I'm rebuilding the new garage. I have to do it right, you know? 

Actually, speaking of the garage, you wouldn't believe the lumber they try to sell you these days. I was down at the hardware store Tuesday, and the two-by-fours were so warped they looked like rocking chair runners. I told the kid working the aisle—must have been nineteen, tops—I said, "If you tried to build a wall with this, it'd look like a funhouse." He just stared at me. Kids today, they just don't know how to work with their hands anymore. My grandson is the same way, always staring at that tablet of his... playing those games where you just tap the screen. I don't see the point. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Right, the move, the garage... and I'm organizing things at church, too. The committee is practically useless without me pushing them along. And on top of it all, I'm still at the plant. I do industrial mixing and blending, have for years, and I still have to be there to show the younger fellows at work how the job actually ought to be done. If I don't watch them, they'll mess up the calibration. We had a guy back in '94, didn't check the grinding pressure, ruined a whole silo of material. Took us three weeks to clean the dust out of the vents. It got into my truck, too, a blue Ford I had back then. Great truck. 

So... yeah, I'm just getting things done, but they made me come in to talk to you about it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated, overactive presentation may be due to a medical condition such as a neurocognitive disorder rather than a primary mood episode.
doctor.question: Have you been having problems with your memory lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory problems, which is not covered by any of the symptoms in the provided profile (which focus on manic symptoms like elevated mood, increased activity, pressured speech, distractibility, etc.).

patient.answer: Memory? No, no, my memory's sharp as a tack. I mean, I can remember things from way back, clear as day. Like that blue Ford I mentioned... 1988 F-150, straight six engine. You couldn't kill that truck. I used to take it up to the lake on weekends. We had this little cabin up there, well, more of a shack really, but we loved it. The water was so clear you could see the rocks on the bottom. We'd fish for bass right off the dock. My buddy Tom, he caught a five-pounder out there once. Tom... he moved out to Arizona a few years back. Says the dry heat is good for his joints. I don't know about that, I think I'd miss the changing seasons. The leaves turning in the fall... there's nothing like it. But yeah, no, my memory is just fine. Why, did someone say I was forgetting things?

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a sustained decreased need for sleep, which would strongly support a manic episode over dementia or mood disorder due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: Have you been needing much less sleep than usual lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about decreased need for sleep, which is a common symptom of mania, but it is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer: Sleep? Well, I haven't really noticed needing any less, no. I mean, I sleep when I need to, you know? Usually, I'm up before the sun anyway, always have been. My dad was the same way. He used to say, "The best part of the day is before the rest of the world wakes up to ruin it." He was a milkman, actually. Back when they still delivered milk in those glass bottles right to your porch. You remember those? They had that little paper cap on top. In the winter, the cream would freeze and push the cap right up out of the bottle. We used to fight over who got to eat the frozen cream... tasted like ice cream if you put a little sugar on it. Dad had this route that took him all the way out past the county line. Sometimes he'd let me ride along in the truck. It smelled like cold metal and sour milk, but I loved it. We'd listen to the radio... mostly baseball games. I still listen to the games on the radio sometimes. It's better than TV, you have to use your imagination. But yeah, no, sleep hasn't really been an issue.

doctor.intent: Assess for elevated or expansive mood to distinguish a primary manic/hypomanic episode from dementia-related disinhibition or personality change.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually cheerful or high lately?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been feeling like everybody needs to either get on board with my plans or get out of my way, and I’ll go from joking and feeling ten feet tall to snapping at my wife or my boy over some little question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has been feeling 'unusually cheerful or high lately', which directly maps to the Elevated_Irritable_Mood symptom asking about abnormally and persistently elevated or expansive mood.

patient.answer:
Cheerful? High? I don't know about cheerful, but I've been feeling... well, I feel ten feet tall. Like I've got all the answers and everyone else is just dragging their feet. I mean, I'll be joking around, feeling great, but then somebody will ask me some stupid little question and I just snap. Like my wife, or my boy, they'll interrupt me when I'm drawing up the plans for the garage and I just tell them, you either need to get on board with what I'm doing or get out of my way! 

Speaking of getting out of the way, you should see the traffic out on Route 9 these days. Used to be you could cruise all the way into town without hitting a single red light. Now? They put in three new subdivisions out past the old drive-in theater, and it's just bumper to bumper. The drive-in... man, we used to go there every Friday night when I was in high school. You could fit six people in the trunk of a Buick if you knew how to pack 'em right. We'd watch those old monster movies, the ones where the zipper on the rubber suit was still showing. We thought it was the funniest thing in the world. We'd get popcorn that tasted like cardboard and those big sodas in the wax paper cups. They don't make cups like that anymore. Now everything is plastic. Plastic this, plastic that. It's ruining the oceans, you know. I saw a documentary about it on public television. The turtles... they think the plastic bags are jellyfish. It's a shame, really, what we're doing to the planet. But anyway, yeah, I've just been feeling like I'm the only one who knows what's going on, and everyone else is just in the way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a secondary medical or neurologic cause for the mood symptoms, which would help distinguish a primary manic episode from an organic mood disorder or dementia-related behavioral change.
doctor.question: Have you had any recent medical illness or brain problem, like a stroke or head injury?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recent medical illnesses or brain problems (like a stroke or head injury) to rule out organic causes for the symptoms. The symptom profile does not contain an item related to medical history or organic causes.

patient.answer: Medical illness? Stroke? No, nothing like that. My brain's working better than ever, actually. I haven't been to a hospital since... well, since they took my appendix out back in '92. Or was it '93? It was right around the time the Blue Jays won the World Series, I remember that much because I was watching the game on this tiny little TV they had mounted up in the corner of the hospital room. Joe Carter hit that walk-off home run... man, what a moment. I used to play a little baseball myself, you know. Third base. They called me the "Hot Corner" because nothing got past me. I had this old leather mitt that I oiled every single week. Smelled like neat's-foot oil and dirt. You can't buy a glove like that anymore, everything now is synthetic. Just like those plastic cups I was telling you about. It's all connected, really. The synthetic gloves, the plastic in the ocean, the way people just don't take pride in their work anymore. Back when I was at the plant, running the grinders, you had to know your machine. You had to feel the vibration in the floor to know if the mix was right. But no, no head injuries or strokes or anything. Why, do I look like I had a stroke?

doctor.intent: Assess whether there is a recent baseline cognitive decline to distinguish a primary manic episode from dementia-related behavioral disturbance.
doctor.question: Have you been getting lost in places that should be familiar to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about getting lost in familiar places, which is a symptom of cognitive impairment or dementia. This is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile (Elevated_Irritable_Mood, Increased_Activity, Pressured_Speech, Manic_Distractibility, Increased_Goal_Activity, Painful_Consequence_Behavior, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer: Lost? Me? No, no, I know exactly where I am and where I'm going. Always have. I've got an internal compass, like a homing pigeon. You know, they used to use pigeons to carry messages during the war. Remarkable creatures, really. People call them "rats with wings" now, but they saved lives. My uncle was in the Signal Corps, actually. He used to tell stories about the equipment they lugged around... radios the size of a suitcase. Now everyone's got a computer in their pocket. It's too much, if you ask me. People walking around, staring at their hands, bumping into each other. Nobody looks up at the sky anymore. The sky out past the county line, where my dad used to drive the milk truck, it was something else. You could see every star. So no, I don't get lost. I know every backroad in this county better than the people who paved them.

doctor.intent: Determine whether his speech/thought process is abnormally increased and hard to interrupt, which would help distinguish mania/hypomania from dementia-related disinhibition or irritability.
doctor.question: Have people been telling you that you’re talking more than usual?

target_item.name: Pressured_Speech
target_item.manifestation: Once I start explaining what needs doing, the words just keep coming, and my family says I talk over them so fast they can’t even tell me to stop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if people have noticed the patient talking more than usual, which directly matches the Pressured_Speech symptom where the patient is more talkative than usual or feels pressure to keep talking.

patient.answer: Well, yeah, I suppose. Once I start explaining what needs doing, the words just keep coming, you know? My family, they complain that I talk over them so fast they can’t even tell me to stop. But I've got a lot of important things to get out! It's like I'm an auctioneer. You ever listen to those guys? Man, they can really rattle it off. We used to go to the livestock and equipment auctions out past the county line when I was a kid. My dad would bid on these old tractors, International Harvesters, mostly. Red as a candy apple. The sound of those old engines, that deep, heavy chug-chug-chug... you just don't hear machinery like that anymore. Now it's all electric this and hybrid that. Silent. You can't even hear a car coming up behind you in the grocery store parking lot! I almost got clipped by one of those little silent cars at the supermarket last Tuesday. And don't get me started on the supermarket, they moved the coffee aisle clear to the other side of the building and didn't put up a single sign to tell anybody where the Folgers went.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this elevated, pressured, tangential state is a first manic episode or part of a history of recurrent bipolar episodes.
doctor.question: Have you ever had another period in your life when you felt this same way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past episodes of similar symptoms (history of manic/hypomanic episodes). My symptom profile covers my current symptoms (Elevated_Irritable_Mood, Increased_Activity, etc.) and duration, but does not explicitly contain information about past psychiatric history or previous similar episodes.

patient.answer: Another period? Well, I don't know, maybe? I mean, I always feel pretty good, but this... this is like my engine's been overhauled and running on premium fuel, you know? Premium fuel. I used to go to this old filling station on Route 9, back when they actually pumped your gas for you. Guy named Earl ran it. He had this little bell that would ding-ding when you rolled over the black hose, and he'd come out with a rag in his back pocket, wipe down your windshield, check your oil. Full service, they called it. Now you gotta freeze your hands off pumping it yourself, and half the time the screen on the pump is broken or asking if you want a car wash. Car washes! They used to have high school kids doing car washes on Saturdays to raise money for the band uniforms. My nephew played the trombone in the marching band. Big, brass thing. He was always complaining about how heavy it was to carry in the summer heat, especially during the Fourth of July parade. They always marched right down Main Street, right past the old courthouse with the clock tower. They don't make clocks like that anymore, all gears and heavy weights. It's all digital now, just blinking numbers. Blinking numbers everywhere you look. But, uh, what were you asking me? About feeling this way? I don't know, I just feel like I've got a lot of energy right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a distinct episode of elevated or irritable mood lasting at least one week, which best separates a primary manic episode from chronic personality/style issues or neurocognitive causes.
doctor.question: How long have you been feeling this unusually energized and driven?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a month, since we were forced to start leaving the old house.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the length of time the patient has been experiencing the symptoms ('How long have you been feeling this unusually energized and driven?'), which corresponds to the 'duration' item.

patient.answer: Well, I'd say it's been about a month now. Ever since they made us start packing up to leave the old house. It's a shame, really, having to leave that place. The foundation was solid block, not like the cheap poured concrete they use in these new subdivisions. You know, I used to work the big industrial mixers, grinding and blending the aggregates for concrete down at the plant. Heavy work, dusty work. You'd come home and blow your nose and it would be gray. But we made good material. Built half the county with it. The bridges, the retaining walls over by the river... The river used to flood every spring before they put in the dam. I remember one year the water came right up to the porch of the old Miller place. They had these beautiful weeping willows in the front yard, just drinking up all that water. Willows are funny trees, they'll find a water pipe and crack it right open if you're not careful. Roots just snake their way in looking for a drink. Kind of like how I feel right now, just reaching out, ready to go, you know? But yeah, about a month, since we had to start moving out.

inference.note: A distinct ~1-month period of increased energy, grandiosity/feeling 'ten feet tall,' pressured/excessive speech, irritability, distractibility, and goal-directed activity supports a manic syndrome. Dementia/vascular dementia options (F02.81, F01.51) are less likely given no clear progressive memory loss, getting lost, stroke history, or other neurocognitive evidence. Bipolar I manic episode vs single manic episode remain, and mood disorder due to another medical condition is less likely but not fully excluded.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been observable cognitive changes suggesting a neurocognitive disorder or mood disorder due to another medical condition rather than a primary bipolar manic episode.
doctor.question: Have your family noticed that your memory or thinking has changed recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in memory or thinking (cognitive changes), which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile (which focus on manic symptoms like elevated mood, increased activity, pressured speech, distractibility, goal-directed activity, painful consequence behavior, functional impairment, and duration).

patient.answer: My memory? Well, I haven't noticed anything wrong with it. I mean, my daughter, she's always harping on me about forgetting where I put my keys, but who doesn't do that? Keys are small, they slip right down into the couch cushions. We had this old plaid couch when she was growing up, ugly thing, green and orange. But comfortable! Man, you could fall asleep on that thing in five minutes flat. We bought it at a yard sale down the street from this couple who were moving to Florida. Florida! Too hot for me. All that humidity, makes you sweat just standing still. And the alligators, you hear about those alligators crawling right up into people's swimming pools? Imagine waking up and finding a ten-foot reptile taking a dip in your backyard. They got those thick scales, like armor. Reminds me of the heavy equipment we used to use down at the mixing plant, big armored machines. You had to grease the joints on those things every single day or they'd seize up on you right in the middle of a job. Nothing worse than a seized bearing when you've got a deadline. But no, my memory is sharp as a tack. I can remember the serial number off my first car, a '68 Chevy. So I don't know what they're complaining about.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a prior history of manic or hypomanic episodes, which would distinguish bipolar disorder from a single manic episode or a mood disorder due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: Before this past month, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt this unusually energized and driven for several days in a row?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past episodes of mania/hypomania (history of similar symptoms before this past month), which is not covered by the current symptom profile.

patient.answer: Another time? Well, I don't know, maybe? I mean, I've always been a hard worker. You don't last long at the plant if you don't have the drive. The drive... that's what my old foreman used to say. "You gotta have the drive, boys!" He was a tough old bird, missing half his left index finger from a bandsaw accident back in the seventies. The seventies... man, those were different times. You could get a burger, fries, and a shake for under two bucks. We used to go to this drive-in place on Friday nights, they'd bring the food right out to your window on a little tray that hooked onto the door. You had to be careful rolling the window up, though, or the whole thing would spill. My buddy Frank spilled a whole strawberry shake on the interior of his Mustang once. Red interior, too, so you couldn't really see the stain, but the smell... it smelled like sour milk in there for a month. He tried everything to get it out, baking soda, vinegar, you name it. Vinegar is great for cleaning, you know. My mother used to wash the windows with vinegar and newspaper. Said it didn't leave streaks like those chemical sprays. Newspapers used to be so thick, especially the Sunday edition. You'd spend half the morning just reading the comics. Peanuts, Garfield, Family Circus... I always liked the ones with the little dotted lines showing where the kid ran all over the neighborhood. Just like me right now, going a mile a minute! But, uh, what did you ask me? About feeling energized before? I don't know, I've always had a lot of energy.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a recent substance or medication trigger for the manic symptoms, to distinguish a primary manic episode from a substance/medication-induced or other secondary mood disorder.
doctor.question: Have you started any new medicines or drugs recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about new medicines or drugs, which is not covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer: New medicines? No, no, I haven't started anything new. I take my blood pressure pills, always have. The little white ones. They changed the shape of them a few years back, used to be round, now they're sort of oval. Oval... you know, like a football. I used to love watching football on Sundays. The old gridiron. We had this high school coach, Coach Henderson, he made us run drills until we puked. Tough as nails, that guy. He drove this old beat-up Ford pickup, rust all along the wheel wells. You see a lot of rust around here because they salt the roads so heavy in the winter. Salt eats right through the metal if you don't wash it off. We used to use a special sealant on the metal chutes at the mixing plant to keep the aggregate from wearing them down too fast. You had to reapply it every six months or the friction would just grind the steel down to nothing. Steel is strong, but friction... friction always wins eventually. Just wears things away. Kind of like my joints these days, knees popping every time I stand up. But no, no new drugs or anything like that. Just the usual stuff.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this is a first lifetime manic episode or part of bipolar disorder by clarifying any past episodes of similar elevated/irritable energy.
doctor.question: Before this past month, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt unusually energized like this for several days in a row?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past episodes of similar energized behavior (assessing for a history of manic or hypomanic episodes prior to the current episode). None of the symptoms in the profile describe past episodes; they only describe the current episode's symptoms.

patient.answer: Didn't you just ask me that? I swear we just talked about this. Like I was trying to say, I really couldn't tell you if I had times like this before. I don't know, I've just always been a go-getter. You know who else was a go-getter? My brother-in-law, Dave. He sold vacuum cleaners door to door back in the eighties. Those big heavy Kirbys. You ever use a Kirby? Built like a tank, those things. Heavy metal casing, a real solid motor in 'em. Not like the cheap plastic junk they sell today. Everything is plastic now. Plastic bags, plastic bumpers on cars... I remember when cars had real solid chrome bumpers. You get in a fender bender with a '57 Chevy, you'd barely leave a scratch on the bumper, but you'd absolutely total whatever plastic thing they're making nowadays. My neighbor drives one of those little plastic cars. A blue one. Parks it right on the property line, drives me up the wall. I keep telling him, 'Move it over a foot, Bob!' But he's deaf in one ear from his time in the artillery. Artillery is loud, man. Shakes your teeth right out of your head. Makes the ground vibrate... just like the big crushers at the plant. But anyway, yeah, I don't really remember any specific times like you're talking about.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective evidence of a prior manic or hypomanic episode, which would distinguish bipolar disorder from a single manic episode or a mood disorder due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: Has there ever been another time in your life when other people told you that you were acting like this?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past history of similar episodes (specifically, if others have told the patient they were acting like this before). The symptom profile only covers the current episode's symptoms and duration, not past psychiatric history.

patient.answer: Other people telling me? No, nobody's ever said anything like that to me. People used to just mind their own business, you know? Good fences make good neighbors, that's what Robert Frost said. We read him in a literature class I took back at the community college. I only went for a couple semesters, thought about getting a business degree, but then the job at the mixing plant opened up. Good money, union benefits. The union was really strong back then. Local 402. We'd have these meetings down at the VFW hall on Elm Street on Tuesday nights. They served this terrible burnt coffee out of a big silver percolator. Those old percolators always made the coffee taste like aluminum. Aluminum is a funny metal. We used to blend these aluminum oxide powders for polishing compounds at the plant. Real fine dust, gets absolutely everywhere. You'd blow your nose at the end of the shift and the tissue would be sparkling. Sparkles... like the paint on those expensive bass boats. Guys take those out on the lake on weekends, spend twenty thousand dollars just to catch a two-pound fish. Fishing is way too slow for me anyway, sitting out there baking in the sun just waiting for a bobber to move. I like to keep moving, keep my hands busy. But yeah, to answer your question, nobody's ever told me I was acting any kind of way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a prior manic or hypomanic episode, which would distinguish bipolar disorder from a single manic episode and help separate primary mood disorder from secondary causes.
doctor.question: Before this month, was there ever another time in your life when you had several days of this same kind of unusually high energy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past episodes of elevated energy (manic/hypomanic episodes). This relates to psychiatric history, which is not covered in the current symptom profile.

patient.answer: I... wait, are you asking me that again? I feel like I'm stuck on a merry-go-round here. We just went over this, didn't we? I mean, I really don't think so. I don't remember any other time. Like I said, I've always been a guy who likes to keep moving. Moving... you know, kinetic energy. That's what they call it in physics. We had to learn a little bit about that at the plant, how the kinetic energy of the grinding wheels transferred to the aggregate. If the wheels spun too fast, they'd overheat and you'd smell this awful burning rubber smell. Rubber is amazing stuff though, comes right from trees down in South America. They tap them like maple trees up in Vermont. I went to Vermont once, for a fall foliage tour with my late wife, Brenda. Beautiful colors, all reds and oranges. Orange is a tough color to pull off, unless you're wearing hunting gear. I used to go deer hunting with my uncle when I was a teenager. He had this old lever-action Winchester rifle, kicked like a mule. Left a bruise on my shoulder the size of a grapefruit. Grapefruits are too sour for me, honestly. I prefer a nice sweet navel orange. But no, I don't recall any other time with this kind of energy. I'm just... I'm just feeling good right now, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine whether the episode is causing marked functional impairment, which would support mania over hypomania and help distinguish F30.1 from F31.1/F06.30.
doctor.question: Has this past month caused serious problems at home or at work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I ended up getting pulled from work after a safety incident, and at home my wife and family stopped trusting me with decisions about money, driving, or the move because things had gotten out of hand.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the past month has caused serious problems at home or at work, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer: Well, it hasn't been great, I'll tell you that. At work, they actually pulled me off the floor after a safety incident. Just a little misunderstanding with the mixing equipment, but safety first, right? That's what they always say. We used to have these big yellow signs all over the plant: 'Safety First.' Yellow is a good color for that, really catches the eye. Like school buses. Did you know school buses are that specific shade of yellow because it's the easiest color to see in the early morning light? My cousin drove a school bus for thirty years. Thirty years! Can you imagine dealing with screaming kids for that long? Kids these days are always on their phones anyway, not even looking out the window. When I was a kid, we'd play games, you know, punch buggy or whatever. Volkswagen Beetles, they don't make them like they used to. Classic cars had character. Anyway, at home, things are a mess too. My wife and the kids, they basically stopped trusting me with anything. They won't let me make decisions about the money, they don't want me driving, they even took over planning this move we're supposed to be doing. They said things just got out of hand. Hand... you know, human hands are incredibly complex. All those tiny bones and tendons. I read an article once about how surgeons have to practice on grapes to get their hands steady enough. Grapes are mostly water, you know. Good for hydration. But yeah, it's caused some real headaches, both at the plant and at the house.

doctor.intent: Determine whether his elevated/irritable, pressured, tangential state is due to a medical condition rather than a primary mood episode by checking for recent substance exposure that can cause mania-like symptoms.
doctor.question: Have you been using any alcohol or recreational drugs lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about alcohol or recreational drug use, which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer: No, I don't touch any of that. Never had a taste for drugs, and I haven't had a drink in... well, a long time. Used to grab a beer with the guys after a shift at the plant, sure. We'd go down to this place called O'Malley's. They had this beautiful old Wurlitzer jukebox in the corner, played actual vinyl 45s. You just don't see records much anymore, do you? Everything is digital now, floating around in the cloud or whatever they call it. I still don't really understand how a cloud holds information. Real clouds are just water vapor, condensation. You look up on a summer day and see those big puffy cumulus ones, they look like cotton candy. I used to buy cotton candy for the kids at the county fair when they were little. It's just spun sugar, really. Melts the second it hits your tongue. Terrible for your teeth, though. My dentist, Dr. Aris, he's always lecturing me about sugar. He's got these huge hands, feels like he's shoving a baseball mitt in my mouth when he checks my molars. But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right. No, no alcohol or drugs for me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a recent physiologic trigger suggesting a mood disorder due to another medical condition rather than a primary manic episode
doctor.question: Have you had any recent changes in your blood pressure medicine?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recent changes in blood pressure medicine, which is a question about medical history or potential substance/medication effects. This is not covered by any of the specific bipolar symptom items in my profile.

patient.answer: Blood pressure medicine? No, I haven't had any changes to that. Same little white pill I've been taking for years. They make those pills so tiny though, they're hard to pinch out of the bottle with my thick fingers. Pinching... you know, crabs have incredible pinching power in their claws. I went crabbing once down in Maryland with my brother-in-law. You just tie a raw chicken neck to a piece of string and drop it in the water. Chicken is getting so expensive these days at the grocery store, though. Used to be the cheapest meat you could buy. Now everything is expensive because of inflation. A dollar just doesn't stretch like it used to. They used to make dollar bills out of silver certificates, backed by actual silver in the vault. Silver tarnishes, though, you have to polish it to keep it shining. I did a lot of polishing at the plant, actually, getting the metal components smoothed out on the line. You use a high-speed buffing wheel and a special compound for that. The compound smells a bit like wet clay. Clay is what they make bricks out of, baking them in massive kilns... but anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, the blood pressure medicine is exactly the same. No changes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a prior history of depressive episodes, which would distinguish bipolar disorder from a first manic episode or a mood disorder due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period in your life when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of depressive episodes (feeling depressed most of the day for at least two weeks), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer: Depressed? Two weeks? No, I don't think so. I've never really been one to get down in the dumps like that. I mean, everyone has a bad day here and there, sure, but not for weeks on end. Weeks... you know, a fortnight. They still use that word over in England, a fortnight. Fourteen nights. I've always wanted to go to England, see the Tower of London and all that history. History is fascinating, isn't it? The way things were built hundreds of years ago without any of the modern machinery we have today. Like the pyramids in Egypt! How did they move those massive stone blocks? Some people say it was aliens, but I think they just had a really clever system of ramps and pulleys. Pulleys are a simple machine, really. We used a lot of pulleys and hoists at the plant to lift the heavy mixing vats. If one of those cables snapped, watch out. That's why they had all those safety inspections. The inspector, this guy named Gary, he was a real stickler. He'd walk around with his little clipboard and his hard hat, checking every single bolt. Hard hats are important. They save lives. I always wore mine, even when it was hot and sweaty in the summer. Summer heat can really take it out of you, make you feel sluggish. But no, not depressed. I've never had a stretch like that where I just felt low all the time.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this is a first lifetime manic episode or a recurrence, to distinguish single-episode mania from bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: Before this past month, did you ever have another time in your life when you felt this same way for at least a week?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past manic episodes (history of similar symptoms lasting at least a week before the current month). The symptom profile only covers the current symptoms, duration, and functional impairment, not past psychiatric history.

patient.answer: Felt this way before? For a whole week? No, I don't think so. This is really the first time. A week goes by so fast lately anyway. Seven days used to feel like a lifetime when you were working the line, though. We worked six days a week at the plant sometimes, during the busy season. The overtime pay was good, time and a half. I saved up all my overtime and bought a '68 Chevy Impala. Beautiful car. It had this deep blue paint job, almost like the ocean. I've never actually been out on the real ocean, though. I always wanted to take one of those big cruises. You see them on TV, those massive ships with swimming pools and all-you-can-eat buffets right on the deck. I always wonder how a boat that heavy even floats. Displacement, I guess. Archimedes' principle. We learned about that in a physics class I took at the community college back in the seventies.
